title: API design (REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL, pagination, idempotency, versioning, webhooks)
relevance: High — nearly every HLD "design X" round starts with sketching APIs; FAANG and Indian product cos probe protocol choice, pagination, retries/idempotency, and (for payments/integrations) webhooks + versioning.
company_notes: Campus/new-grad HLD almost always includes the define-APIs step (REST + pagination table stakes; naming GraphQL/gRPC separates strong candidates). Mid-level (1–4 YOE) deep-dives cover idempotency, cursor pagination, webhook reliability, and versioning at Stripe-like, marketplace, and platform cos (Amazon, Uber, Atlassian, Flipkart, etc.). Universal building block every design round; dedicated Stripe API/webhook prompts are rarer but patterns appear inside payments, notifications, and marketplaces.

phases.goal: Establish REST, gRPC, and GraphQL models and the interview rule of thumb for where each belongs.

must_hit.point: REST models resources as nouns with HTTP verbs for CRUD, stateless requests, status codes, and cacheable GETs; interview default for public, browser, and mobile APIs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sketches paths like /users/{id}/orders, maps verbs to CRUD, and names REST as the public/edge default.

must_hit.point: RPC/gRPC is action-oriented (e.g. GetUser, ChargeCard); gRPC uses protobuf + HTTP/2 + codegen with unary/streaming and is the default for internal service-to-service when latency, typing, and streaming matter; browsers need gRPC-Web or a gateway.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts method-style RPCs with REST resources and places gRPC inside the datacenter, noting browser/gateway caveats.

must_hit.point: GraphQL lets the client declare response shape on one endpoint, avoiding over/under-fetch for heterogeneous clients, while shifting cost to the server via resolvers, N+1, query cost limits, and harder HTTP caching/rate limits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains single-endpoint client-shaped queries and names server-side costs (N+1, caching, rate limits).

must_hit.point: Rule of thumb: REST at the edge, gRPC inside the datacenter, GraphQL when flexible multi-client fetching (mobile + dashboard) is emphasized — justify rather than cargo-cult.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate assigns protocols by hop with a brief justification instead of picking one protocol for everything.

probes: For a mobile feed, an admin dashboard, and an internal OrderService, which protocol would you put on each hop and why?
When would you reach for GraphQL or gRPC instead of the usual REST public API?

hints.1: Start from who the client is and whether the call is public/browser or internal service-to-service.
hints.2: Map: resource nouns + HTTP at the edge; method/protobuf/streaming inside; client-shaped queries when many clients need different fields.
hints.3: Say REST for public/browser/mobile, gRPC for internal low-latency typed/streaming hops, GraphQL when mobile + dashboard need flexible fetching — and name one downside of each wrong pick.

phases.goal: Check concrete mechanics of pagination, idempotency keys, versioning strategies, and webhook delivery hygiene.

must_hit.point: Offset/page pagination is simple and supports jump-to-page, but deep OFFSET gets slow and concurrent inserts can cause duplicates/skips; fine for small admin lists.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks offset for admin page jumps and names slow deep OFFSET plus duplicate/skip risk under concurrent writes.

must_hit.point: Cursor/keyset pagination uses an opaque cursor encoding last sort key(s), seeks with indexed WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT, stays stable for feeds/infinite scroll, cannot random-jump pages, should cap limit, and prefer has_next over expensive COUNT(*).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes cursor encoding last keys, index seek query shape, and has_next instead of COUNT(*) for feeds.

must_hit.point: GET/PUT/DELETE are naturally retry-safe; POST create/charge needs a client idempotency key (UUID) so timeout retries do not double-charge; server stores first status+body by key (+ request fingerprint); same key with different body is a conflict.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks Idempotency-Key lookup → replay first success → same key different body → conflict (e.g. 409).

must_hit.point: Prefer additive versioning (new optional fields/endpoints); strategies include URL /v1, header (Accept / Stripe-Version), or date-pinned account versions; breaking changes need a new version plus deprecation window rather than a light big-bang /v2 rewrite.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names additive-first changes and at least one of URL, header, or Stripe-style date-pinned versions with a deprecation path for breaks.

must_hit.point: Webhooks push events to subscriber URLs (vs polling); must HMAC-verify signatures over HTTPS, return fast 2xx then process async, retry with backoff, dedupe on delivery/event id, and ignore unknown event types gracefully.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sequences verify signature → fast 2xx → enqueue/async → dedupe by event/delivery id → retries/backoff.

probes: News feed vs admin page 47 of users — cursor or offset, and what does the cursor DB query look like?
Client POSTs /payments, times out, retries — how does Idempotency-Key prevent double-charge, and what if the retry body differs?
Stripe payment_intent.succeeded hits your endpoint — what is the correct verify → respond → process sequence?

hints.1: Separate read-list UX (jump to page vs infinite scroll) from write-safety (retries) and push delivery (webhooks).
hints.2: Offset for small admin jumps; cursor for feeds; Idempotency-Key store for POST; HMAC + fast 2xx + async for webhooks.
hints.3: Cursor: opaque last sort keys + indexed seek + has_next. Idempotency: store first response; same key different body → 409. Webhooks: verify → 2xx → queue → dedupe; handler failure after 2xx is covered by provider retries + your dedupe.

phases.goal: Force justified protocol and pagination choices and surface why GraphQL/gRPC are not universal defaults.

must_hit.point: GraphQL everywhere is a weak default because of caching difficulty, per-field authz, abusive nested queries, and operational complexity; REST is often enough.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate argues against GraphQL-by-default citing caching, authz, nested-query abuse, and ops cost.

must_hit.point: gRPC is not always faster in designs: protobuf/HTTP/2 help, but most systems are not serialization-bound; public API ergonomics and CDN caching often favor REST/JSON.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates wire efficiency from end-to-end bottlenecks and keeps REST/JSON at the public/CDN edge.

must_hit.point: On a hot write-heavy feed, offset pagination is the wrong default; interviewers expect cursor plus an explanation of duplicates/skips under concurrent writes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects offset for hot feeds and explains concurrent-insert duplicate/skip behavior favoring cursor/keyset.

probes: Why not use GraphQL for every client-facing API?
Is gRPC always the faster choice for public APIs?
Why is offset pagination risky on a write-heavy feed?

hints.1: Ask what becomes harder once you leave plain HTTP resource GETs.
hints.2: Compare caching/CDN and public ergonomics vs flexible queries and binary internal RPCs.
hints.3: GraphQL: caching, field authz, nested abuse, ops. gRPC: not serialization-bound; REST/JSON wins at public CDN edge. Offset on hot feeds: duplicates/skips → use cursor.

phases.goal: Apply protocol choice, REST sketching, idempotency, versioning, and webhooks inside a concrete design round.

must_hit.point: Protocol pick drill: assign REST / GraphQL / gRPC across mobile feed, admin dashboard, and internal OrderService and name one downside of picking wrong on a hop.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a hop-by-hop assignment with at least one concrete failure mode for a wrong protocol.

must_hit.point: REST sketch for Ticketmaster-lite: noun resources and methods for search events, hold seat, confirm payment, including status codes such as 201, 409 hold conflict, and 429.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketches resource paths/verbs and uses 201 on create, 409 on hold conflict, 429 on rate limit.

must_hit.point: Versioning drill: renaming verified: bool to status: enum breaks old clients; Stripe-style version transforms or a /v2 path can keep old clients working during evolution.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains the break, then either date/header version transforms or dual /v1 vs /v2 with deprecation rather than silent field removal.

must_hit.point: Webhook failure after 200: provider will retry; correct design still dedupes on event id so processing stays once-only despite post-ack handler failure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States fast 200/2xx then async, and that retries plus event-id dedupe handle failure after ack.

probes: Design Ticketmaster-lite booking APIs — resources, methods, and key status codes for hold conflicts and rate limits.
You rename verified: bool to status: enum — what breaks, and how do Stripe-style transforms or /v2 help?
If your webhook handler fails after returning 200, how do you still process the event exactly once?

hints.1: Sketch contracts before boxes: nouns/verbs first, then retries and evolution.
hints.2: Use REST nouns for booking; Idempotency-Key on payment confirm; additive or versioned fields for renames; verify+ack+dedupe for webhooks.
hints.3: Hold conflict → 409, create → 201, throttle → 429; bool→enum needs /v2 or version transforms; after 200, provider retries + event-id dedupe give at-least-once delivery with once-only side effects.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: REST is the interview default for public/browser/mobile APIs with cacheable GETs and simpler ops; GraphQL wins when heterogeneous clients (mobile + dashboard) need flexible shapes and you accept server costs: resolvers, N+1, query cost limits, and harder HTTP caching/rate limits. Not GraphQL everywhere — caching, per-field authz, abusive nested queries, and operational complexity often make REST enough.

REST/JSON at the edge for public ergonomics and CDN caching; gRPC (protobuf + HTTP/2 + codegen + streaming) inside the datacenter for typed, low-latency service-to-service calls. gRPC is not always faster end-to-end because most designs are not serialization-bound; browsers need gRPC-Web or a gateway.

Offset/page is simple and supports jump to page N (e.g. admin lists) but deep OFFSET slows down and concurrent inserts cause duplicates/skips — bad on hot write-heavy feeds. Cursor/keyset encodes last sort keys, seeks via index, stabilizes feeds/infinite scroll, forgoes random page jumps, caps limit, and prefers has_next over expensive COUNT(*).

Webhooks push events to subscriber URLs instead of client polling; require HMAC signature verification, HTTPS, fast 2xx then async work, retries with backoff, and dedupe on delivery/event id, while ignoring unknown event types gracefully.

Prefer additive changes (new optional fields/endpoints). Version via URL /v1, headers (Accept / Stripe-Version), or date-pinned account versions; breaking changes get a new version plus deprecation window — do not force big-bang /v2 rewrites lightly or silently remove fields from mobile clients.

gotchas.trap: Defaulting to GraphQL everywhere for client APIs
gotchas.correction: Call out caching difficulty, per-field authz, abusive nested queries, and operational complexity; REST is often enough unless flexible multi-client fetching is a real requirement.
Protobuf/HTTP/2 help, but most designs are not serialization-bound; public ergonomics and CDN caching often favor REST/JSON at the edge.

gotchas.trap: Using offset pagination on a hot write-heavy feed
gotchas.correction: Expect cursor/keyset and an explanation of duplicates/skips under concurrent writes; reserve offset for small admin jump-to-page lists.

gotchas.trap: Retrying non-idempotent POSTs without idempotency keys
gotchas.correction: Classic double-charge / double-booking mode; require client Idempotency-Key (UUID), store first status+body, and conflict when the same key arrives with a different body.

gotchas.trap: Webhooks without signature checks or with heavy sync work in the request path
gotchas.correction: Verify HMAC signatures over HTTPS, return fast 2xx then enqueue/async process; otherwise you get spoofing and timeout-driven retry storms.

gotchas.trap: Breaking mobile clients with silent field removals
gotchas.correction: Evolve additively or version deliberately (header/URL/date-pinned) and sunset old versions on purpose rather than renaming/removing fields in place.
